extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of moral/political philosophy, legislators, policymakers, and theorists of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Methodological guidance for forming and evaluating rules (arts, policy, and morality): how ends should be defined, how scientific knowledge supplies means, and how to convert theoretical truths into practical precepts. Targets lawmakers, moral philosophers, and practical craftsmen who must reconcile scientific knowledge with prescriptive rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground rules of art in scientific theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: “The grounds, then, of every rule of art, are to be found in the theorems of science.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rule of practice must be justified by the corresponding scientific theorems that show which causes produce the desired effects. Art supplies the desirable end (major premise); science supplies the proposition that certain actions will attain that end. Practitioners (e.g., legislators) should therefore examine the reasons of maxims rather than treat maxims as final. Example contrast: judges (apply law syllogistically) vs. legislators (must inspect grounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define ends as the exclusive province of art
rubrics_metrics.description: “The definition of the end itself belongs exclusively to Art, and forms its peculiar province.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining what is desirable (the major premise: what ought to be pursued) is not a scientific task. Producers of rules must state clear ends before consulting science about means. Ends require justification by general premises (teleological principles) to allow consistent ordering among competing ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not convert a theorem into a precept until all necessary conditions are known
rubrics_metrics.description: A speculative theorem is not ripe for being turned into a precept until the whole, and not a part merely, of the operation which belongs to science, has been performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ascertain both positive causes and all negative/counteracting conditions (circumstances that would prevent the desired effect). If a rule is framed prematurely, overlooked counteracting causes will cause failure and force re-opening of the scientific inquiry. Practical implication: complete the relevant scientific investigation before making definitive rules for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that practical rules are necessarily imperfect and provisional
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of art do not attempt to comprise more conditions than require to be attended to in ordinary cases; and are therefore always imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For usability, rules must be concise and cover ordinary occurrences only; including all contingencies would make rules too cumbersome. In simple manual arts rules may suffice; in complex social/political affairs rules must be treated as provisional heuristics and used with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constantly refer rules back to scientific principles for modification or exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the complicated affairs of life, and still more in those of states and societies, rules can not be relied on, without constantly referring back to the scientific laws on which they are founded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practitioners use rules as default guides but re-examine the scientific bases when unusual circumstances arise. Knowing which practical contingencies require modification or exception involves understanding the theoretical grounds (what combinations of circumstances interfere with the law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deducing specific conduct solely from universal practical maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: The error... of those who would deduce the line of conduct proper to particular cases from supposed universal practical maxims, overlooking the necessity of constantly referring back to the principles of the speculative science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reason downward from abstract principles to particular prescriptions without testing against scientific grounds and considering conflicting ends. The 'geometrical' habit (treating practical maxims as ultimate premises) is criticized as leading to pedantry and bad practical outcomes (example: sweeping political maxims in journalism/political oratory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose an art from rules plus the speculative propositions that justify them
rubrics_metrics.description: An art, or a body of art, consists of the rules, together with as much of the speculative propositions as comprises the justification of those rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete practical guidance should pair prescriptive maxims with the scientific explanations and conditions that justify them. Producers of an 'art' should select from science the propositions necessary to show on what conditions the desired effects depend, so practitioners can judge applicability and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame intermediate (generalia) scientific principles linking science and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: There is need of a set of intermediate scientific truths, derived from the higher generalities of science, and destined to serve as the generalia or first principles of the various arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After defining the end and the set of conditions on which it depends, survey available means and express their relation to the end in a few broad propositions. These intermediate principles make it practical to derive methods as corollaries and are an essential step from abstract science to usable art (example: Monge’s descriptive geometry as a model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge that art traces one effect to many causes while science traces a cause to many effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Science, therefore, following one cause to its various effects, while art traces one effect to its multiplied and diversified causes...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical method requires assembling heterogeneous scientific truths from disparate parts of science to produce the multiple conditions necessary for an effect. This multidisciplinary synthesis should guide rule-formation and reveal practical contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an ultimate teleological standard (promotion of happiness) for testing ends
rubrics_metrics.description: I merely declare my conviction, that the general principle to which all rules of practice ought to conform... is that of conduciveness to the happiness of mankind, or rather, of all sentient beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill recommends promotion of happiness as the controlling standard for judging and ordering ends in morality, prudence, policy, and taste. While not asserting happiness as the sole immediate end of all actions, it is proposed as the ultimate test for whether ends and rules are justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insist on a single ultimate standard of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be some standard by which to determine the goodness or badness, absolute and comparative, of ends... And whatever that standard is, there can be but one;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid conflicting justifications where the same conduct could be approved by one principle and condemned by another, moral theory should posit one ultimate principle (or else require an overarching umpire). This motivates seeking a unified teleological criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let scientific competence substitute for justification of ends
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific observer or reasoner, merely as such, is not an adviser for practice... Whether the ends themselves are such as ought to be pursued... it is no part of his business as a cultivator of science to decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists must avoid overstepping into prescribing ends simply because they can show means to them. The justification of approbation (why an end deserves pursuit) requires teleological premises; practitioners should demand such justification rather than accept scientists' normative claims unexamined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish general premises determining proper objects of approbation and their precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of practice, every one must be required to justify his approbation; and for this there is need of general premises, determining what are the proper objects of approbation, and what the proper order of precedence among those objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers of moral or policy rules must supply or appeal to higher-order principles that rank ends and explain why certain ends take priority in conflicts. Without such ordering, rules lack a defensible foundation for resolving trade-offs.
